events.title: Sugambrian raid on Atuatuca
events.summary: While Caesar ravaged the Eburones, 2,000 Sugambrian horsemen crossed the Rhine to plunder, learned that Caesar's baggage was at Atuatuca under Quintus Cicero, and nearly stormed the camp, destroying two cohorts of recruits caught foraging. The centurion Publius Sextius Baculus, sick in his tent, held the gate.

battle.significance: Caesar's own lesson on the dangers of dispersing troops.

events.title: Caesar executes Acco at Durocortorum
events.summary: At a council of Gaul at Durocortorum (Reims) in autumn 53, Caesar tried the Senonian leader Acco for conspiracy and had him flogged to death 'in the ancestral manner'. The execution of a Gallic noble horrified the Gallic aristocracy and helped spark the general revolt of 52.

events.title: Crassus' head and Euripides' Bacchae
events.summary: When Surena's messenger arrived at the Armenian court, where Orodes was celebrating a marriage alliance with Artavasdes II, a performance of Euripides' Bacchae was under way. The actor Jason of Tralles took Crassus' head and sang Agave's lines over it as if it were Pentheus'. Surena meanwhile staged a mock triumph at Seleucia with a Roman captive dressed as Crassus.

events.title: Death of Crassus at the parley
events.summary: Retreating from Carrhae toward the Armenian hills, Crassus was forced by his mutinous soldiers to accept Surena's offer of a parley. In a scuffle over the horse brought for him, Crassus and his officers were killed. His head and hand were sent to King Orodes.
events.detail: Of perhaps 40,000 men, some 20,000 died and 10,000 were taken prisoner and settled at Merv (Antiochia Margiana); Cassius led about 500 horsemen to Syria. The legionary standards became the most famous of all Roman war trophies until their return to Augustus in 20 BC. The fanciful story that the Parthians poured molten gold into Crassus' mouth is late (Dio).
events.debate: Exact date (9 June is sometimes given for Carrhae; the parley followed within days) and place are uncertain.

events.title: The law of the ten tribunes
events.summary: With Pompey's backing all ten tribunes carried a law permitting Caesar to stand for a second consulship in absence, so that he could pass directly from his Gallic command to office without becoming a private citizen exposed to prosecution. Pompey's subsequent lex de iure magistratuum seemed to cancel it, and he added a clause exempting Caesar by hand after it was engraved.
events.detail: The 'ratio absentis' became the legal crux of the crisis of 50-49: Caesar's opponents argued it had been superseded and that his command could be terminated as early as 1 March 50. Modern discussion (Gelzer, Seager, Morstein-Marx) turns on when his command legally expired, which the sources leave unclear.
events.debate: Terminal date of Caesar's Gallic command (1 March 50 or the end of 50 or 49) is one of the most debated problems of Republican history.

events.title: Lex Pompeia de provinciis: the five-year interval
events.summary: Following a senatus consultum of 53, Pompey's law required a five-year gap between holding a consulship or praetorship and a provincial command, filling the gap in the meantime with ex-magistrates who had not yet governed. It ended the link between office and immediate provincial enrichment that drove bribery, and forced men like Cicero and Bibulus to govern in 51.
events.detail: The law also mattered for Caesar: once there was no requirement that a successor be a magistrate of a particular year, the Senate could name a successor to Gaul at any time. Augustus adopted the five-year interval for senatorial provinces in 27.

events.title: Caesar crosses the Cevennes in winter
events.summary: Hearing that Lucterius of the Cadurci was threatening the province, Caesar secured Narbo and then had his men clear six feet of snow to cross the Cevennes into Arvernian territory, forcing Vercingetorix to turn back to defend his home. Caesar then rode with a small escort through Aeduan country to join his legions.

events.title: Vellaunodunum, Cenabum and Noviodunum
events.summary: In a rapid winter march Caesar took the Senonian town of Vellaunodunum in two days, burned Cenabum in revenge for the massacre of Roman traders, and was accepting the surrender of Noviodunum of the Bituriges when Vercingetorix's cavalry appeared; the townsmen took up arms again until Caesar's German horse drove the Gauls off.

battle.significance: Led Vercingetorix to adopt a scorched-earth strategy.

events.title: Litaviccus leads the Aedui into revolt
events.summary: During the siege of Gergovia the Aeduan noble Litaviccus, bribed by the Arverni, led 10,000 Aeduan infantry marching to join Caesar into revolt by claiming Caesar had murdered their leaders. Caesar intercepted them with four legions, showing them the 'murdered' Eporedorix and Viridomarus alive; Litaviccus fled to Gergovia. The Aedui defected anyway after Caesar's repulse.

events.title: Council of Bibracte confirms Vercingetorix
events.summary: After the Aedui seized Noviodunum with Caesar's hostages, treasury and remounts, a council of all Gaul at Bibracte confirmed Vercingetorix as supreme commander, to the chagrin of the Aeduan leaders. Only the Remi, Lingones and Treveri stayed away. Vercingetorix demanded 15,000 cavalry.

events.title: The cavalry battle before Alesia
events.summary: As Caesar marched toward the province through the land of the Lingones, Vercingetorix attacked his column with his cavalry, whose leaders had sworn not to return home unless they rode twice through the Roman army. Caesar's German horsemen routed them, and Vercingetorix fell back to Alesia.

sides.strength: army on the march, German cavalry

battle.significance: Turned the campaign: Vercingetorix shut himself in Alesia.

events.debate: The site is disputed with the location of Alesia itself; most accept the Vingeanne-Montsaugeon area.

events.title: Pompey marries Cornelia, daughter of Metellus Scipio
events.summary: Declining Caesar's offer of his great-niece Octavia, Pompey married Cornelia, widow of Publius Crassus and daughter of Quintus Caecilius Metellus Pius Scipio, and made her father his colleague as consul for the last five months of 52. The marriage marked his realignment with the optimates.

events.title: The trial of Milo: Pro Milone
events.summary: Tried under Pompey's new law on violence before a court ringed by Pompey's soldiers, Milo was convicted 38 to 13. Cicero, unnerved by the soldiers and the Clodian crowd, delivered his defence badly; he later published the polished Pro Milone, arguing Clodius' death was lawful self-defence. Milo, in exile at Massilia, said that if Cicero had spoken that way he would not be eating such good mullets.
events.detail: Asconius' commentary, written for his sons in the 50s AD, is the best account of any Roman trial: it gives the timeline of the brawl at Bovillae on 18 January, the jurors' votes by order (senators 12-6, equites 13-4, tribuni aerarii 13-3 for conviction), and the procedure under the lex Pompeia de vi with its limits on speech length. The surviving speech, with its 'silent enim leges inter arma', became a model of forensic rhetoric.

events.title: Siege of Lemonum
events.summary: Dumnacus of the Andes besieged Duratius, a pro-Roman leader of the Pictones, in Lemonum (Poitiers); Caninius Rebilus and Gaius Fabius relieved the town and caught Dumnacus' army crossing the Loire, killing 12,000. Survivors under Drappes and Lucterius fled south to Uxellodunum.

sides.strength: two legions under Caninius, 25 cohorts under Fabius

events.title: Campaign against the Bellovaci
events.summary: The Bellovaci under Correus and the Atrebatian Commius held a fortified hill against Caesar and four legions; when Caesar built a causeway and siege works, they escaped behind a screen of burning bundles and staged an ambush in which Correus refused to surrender and was killed.

events.title: Cicero takes Pindenissum
events.summary: As proconsul of Cilicia, Cicero campaigned against the 'Free Cilicians' of the Amanus, was hailed imperator by his troops near Issus, and besieged the mountain town of Pindenissum for 57 days with siege towers and mantlets, selling its people as slaves on the Saturnalia. He spent the next years seeking a triumph for it.

sides.strength: two weak legions and allied troops

events.title: Marcellus flogs a citizen of Novum Comum
events.summary: To deny the validity of the Latin rights and citizenship Caesar had given the Transpadane colony of Novum Comum, the consul Marcus Claudius Marcellus had a former magistrate of Comum flogged and told him to show his scars to Caesar. Cicero thought it outrageous; the man would have been immune as a citizen.

events.title: Cicero publishes De re publica
events.summary: Cicero's six-book dialogue on the best constitution, set in 129 at the house of Scipio Aemilianus, argued that Rome's mixed constitution was the best and imagined a rector or princeps guiding the state; it ended with the Dream of Scipio. It was a success on publication; most of it was lost until Angelo Mai found a palimpsest in the Vatican in 1819.
events.detail: Composed 54-51, it reflects Cicero's anxiety about the dynasts. The Somnium Scipionis survived separately through Macrobius' commentary and shaped medieval cosmology. Whether the 'princeps' of Books 5-6 anticipates Pompey or Augustus has been debated since the nineteenth century.

events.title: Death of Ptolemy XII; Cleopatra VII and Ptolemy XIII succeed
events.summary: Ptolemy XII died early in 51, leaving his kingdom by will to his eldest surviving daughter Cleopatra, about eighteen, and elder son Ptolemy XIII, about ten, under the guardianship of the Roman people; a copy of the will was sent to Rome and lodged with Pompey. Within two years the boy's regents Pothinus and Achillas had driven Cleopatra out.
events.detail: A papyrus decree of 50 BC concerning grain shipments shows the queen's name ahead of her brother's at first, and early dated documents suggest Cleopatra ruled alone in 51-50. The Buchis bull stele of Hermonthis claims she personally rowed the sacred bull to its installation in her first regnal year. Low Nile floods in 50-48 caused famine, weakening her position.
events.debate: The precise date of Auletes' death (before 22 March 51, per a Buchis stele) and the length of Cleopatra's sole rule are debated.

events.title: Curio goes over to Caesar
events.summary: The tribune Gaius Scribonius Curio, elected as an opponent of Caesar, swung to Caesar early in 50, allegedly after Caesar paid his debts of 60 million sesterces (some say 10 million). He then vetoed every attempt to name a successor to Caesar, proposing instead that Caesar and Pompey both give up their armies.

events.title: Pompey's illness at Naples and the prayers of Italy
events.summary: When Pompey fell seriously ill at Naples in 50, the towns of Italy held public prayers and celebrations for his recovery. Plutarch says the enthusiasm misled him into believing that he had only to stamp his foot to raise armies throughout Italy.

events.title: Caesar surrenders two legions for a Parthian war
events.summary: The Senate decreed that Caesar and Pompey each provide one legion for the Parthian war; Pompey asked for the return of the legion he had lent Caesar in 53, so Caesar lost two. He paid each soldier 250 denarii. The legions were kept in Italy at Capua, and Caesar's partisans treated it as proof of bad faith.

events.title: The severe censorship of Appius Claudius
events.summary: Appius Claudius Pulcher, censor with Lucius Calpurnius Piso, struck many senators and equites off the rolls for debt or misconduct, among them the historian Sallust, thereby driving several into Caesar's camp. His fellow censor Piso, Caesar's father-in-law, blocked the expulsion of Curio.

events.title: Philodemus and the library at Herculaneum
events.summary: The Epicurean philosopher Philodemus of Gadara lived under the patronage of Lucius Calpurnius Piso Caesoninus, whose villa at Herculaneum, buried in AD 79, has yielded some 1,800 carbonised papyrus rolls, largely Philodemus' own works on poetry, music, rhetoric, anger and death. Cicero mocked the relationship in In Pisonem.
events.detail: The papyri, found in 1752-54, are the only intact library to survive from antiquity; since 2023 machine learning applied to X-ray scans has begun to read unopened scrolls. Virgil and Varius studied with Philodemus and Siro in the Epicurean circle on the Bay of Naples.
events.debate: Ownership of the villa by Piso is an inference, widely accepted but unproven.

events.title: Disaster at Curicta: Antonius surrenders in Illyricum
events.summary: Caesar's legate Gaius Antonius, the triumvir's brother, was blockaded on the island of Curicta (Krk) by the Pompeian admirals Marcus Octavius and Lucius Scribonius Libo after Dolabella's fleet was destroyed; he surrendered with fifteen cohorts. One raft of Opitergine troops chose mass suicide rather than surrender.

battle.significance: Gave the Pompeians the Adriatic and delayed Caesar's crossing to Epirus.

events.title: Naval battles off Massilia
events.summary: During the siege of Massilia, Decimus Brutus with twelve hastily built ships beat the Massiliot fleet, reinforced by Domitius Ahenobarbus, in June, and won again in July off Tauroeis against a combined Massiliot and Pompeian fleet under Lucius Nasidius, whose squadron fled.

events.title: Mutiny of the Ninth legion at Placentia
events.summary: Returning from Spain, the Ninth legion mutinied at Placentia, demanding the donative Caesar had promised and discharge. Caesar threatened decimation, then executed twelve ringleaders chosen by lot from the 120 most guilty, one of whom proved to have been absent.

events.title: Curio's victory at Utica
events.summary: Landing in Africa with two of Domitius' surrendered legions, Curio defeated the Pompeian Publius Attius Varus outside Utica, the troops of whose camp reportedly wavered over whether to change sides. Varus fled into Utica, and Curio, misinformed that Juba was far away, marched to the Bagradas.

battle.significance: Prelude to Curio's destruction on the Bagradas.

events.title: Varro surrenders Further Spain
events.summary: After Ilerda, Marcus Terentius Varro, Pompey's legate in Further Spain and Rome's greatest scholar, tried to hold Gades, but Corduba and the towns declared for Caesar and one of his two legions deserted. He surrendered his last legion and the treasury at Corduba. Caesar placed Quintus Cassius Longinus in charge.

events.title: Caesar's debt settlement
events.summary: Faced with a collapse of credit and demands for cancellation of debts (novae tabulae), Caesar as dictator ordered property to be valued at pre-war prices and handed to creditors at that valuation, banned the hoarding of more than 60,000 sesterces in cash, and later deducted interest already paid from principal, cutting debts by about a quarter.
events.detail: The measures disappointed radicals such as Caelius and Dolabella, who agitated for cancellation in 48 and 47, but preserved the property order. Caesar boasted that he had spared creditors' principal; Suetonius estimates the overall reduction at a quarter.

events.title: Pompeians kill Aristobulus II and his son Alexander
events.summary: Caesar freed Aristobulus II, Pompey's captive, to raise Judaea against the Pompeians, but partisans of Pompey poisoned him; his son Alexander was beheaded at Antioch on Pompey's orders by Metellus Scipio. Their deaths left Hyrcanus and Antipater free to side with Caesar.

events.title: Caesar's elephant denarius
events.summary: Caesar's first military coinage of the civil war, struck in vast quantities from 49, shows an elephant trampling a serpent or dragon over the name CAESAR, and on the reverse the pontifical implements. It was minted from the treasury he had seized and is the commonest denarius of the period.
events.debate: Meaning of the elephant (victory over evil, a pun on Punic 'caesai' for elephant per the Historia Augusta, or Africa) is debated.

events.title: Labienus deserts Caesar
events.summary: Within days of the Rubicon, Titus Labienus, Caesar's ablest legate throughout the Gallic War, went over to Pompey, a fellow Picene to whom he probably owed his early career. Caesar sent his baggage after him. Labienus became the most implacable of the Pompeian commanders and died at Munda.

events.title: Caesar's march down the Adriatic
events.summary: From Ariminum Caesar's advance guard occupied Pisaurum, Fanum and Ancona, while Antony took Arretium; Iguvium and Auximum, Pompey's home country, opened their gates, and Pompey's recruiting officers fled. By early February Caesar had the whole Adriatic coast and the loyal veterans of the Eighth and Twelfth legions had joined him.
events.detail: The speed and the lack of resistance shocked Pompey, who had boasted that he could raise legions by stamping his foot. Cicero's letters of these weeks show the panic of the propertied classes and the gradual realisation that Caesar's clemency (he released captured officers unharmed) was a deliberate policy contrasting with memories of Sulla.

events.title: The risings of Caelius and Milo
events.summary: The praetor Marcus Caelius Rufus, frustrated by Caesar's moderate debt policy, proposed remission of rents and debts and, when deposed by the Senate, joined the exiled Milo, who returned to raise gladiators and herdsmen in southern Italy. Milo was killed besieging Compsa, and Caelius near Thurii.

events.title: Caesar sacks Gomphi
events.summary: Retreating into Thessaly after Dyrrhachium, Caesar found Gomphi had closed its gates on news of his defeat; he stormed it in a few hours and gave it to his starving soldiers to plunder, after which Metropolis and other Thessalian towns submitted. Appian describes the army's drunken march out of Gomphi.

battle.significance: Restored morale and supplies before Pharsalus.

events.title: Revolt against Quintus Cassius in Further Spain
events.summary: Quintus Cassius Longinus, Caesar's governor of Further Spain, provoked a conspiracy of provincials at Corduba, was wounded, and then faced the mutiny of two legions under the quaestor Marcellus. Lepidus from Hither Spain mediated; Cassius drowned at the mouth of the Ebro on his way home with his loot.
events.detail: The revolt showed how Caesarian government could alienate even loyal provinces. The disaffected legions later formed the core of the Pompeian army of Gnaeus Pompeius in 46-45.

events.title: Caesar burns the Alexandrian fleet and part of the city
events.summary: To prevent Achillas' forces seizing the 72 warships in the harbour, Caesar set them on fire; the blaze spread to the docks and warehouses. Later writers (Seneca, Plutarch, Dio, Gellius) say that 40,000 books or the Great Library itself burned, though Caesar and Strabo, who used the Museum's resources around 25 BC, are silent.
events.debate: Most scholars think books stored in warehouses near the harbour burned, not the Library itself, which continued to function; Mark Antony's alleged gift of 200,000 scrolls from Pergamon (Plutarch, Antony 58) is reported as a hostile rumour.

events.title: Caesar crosses to Epirus in midwinter
events.summary: With shipping for only seven legions (some 15,000 men) and 500 cavalry, Caesar sailed from Brundisium on 4 January 48 by the unreformed calendar, slipping past Bibulus' fleet of over 100 ships to land at Palaeste on the Ceraunian coast. He took Oricum and Apollonia, but Bibulus burned 30 returning transports and blockaded the rest at Brundisium.
events.detail: The crossing in winter, against a superior fleet, was a typical Caesarian gamble. Plutarch's story belongs here: impatient for reinforcements, Caesar tried to cross back in a small boat in disguise and told the frightened helmsman, 'You carry Caesar and his fortune.' Bibulus died of exhaustion and illness while maintaining the blockade.

events.title: Antony brings the second wave to Nymphaeum
events.summary: After months of waiting, Antony crossed with four legions and 800 cavalry in late March or April, chased by the Pompeian Coponius' Rhodian squadron, which a shift in the wind wrecked on the rocks. He landed at Nymphaeum north of Lissus and joined Caesar despite Pompey's attempt to intercept him.

events.title: Cleopatra comes to Caesar
events.summary: Expelled by her brother's regents and encamped near Pelusium, Cleopatra had herself brought by boat to the palace at night by the Sicilian Apollodorus, concealed, Plutarch says, in a bedding sack. Caesar, who had come to arbitrate under Ptolemy XII's will, sided with her and summoned both siblings.
events.detail: Dio has her win Caesar by her beauty and wit; modern historians stress that Caesar needed Egyptian grain and money (he demanded 17.5 million denarii owed by Auletes) and that Cleopatra was the more capable partner. The carpet of modern films comes from Plutarch's strômatodesmon, a bag for bedding.

events.title: Battle of the Heptastadion: Caesar swims for his life
events.summary: Fighting for the mole (Heptastadion) linking Pharos to the city, Caesar's men were routed by an Egyptian counterattack; the overcrowded boat Caesar boarded capsized and he swam to safety, holding papers above the water and, Suetonius adds, dragging his general's cloak in his teeth. About 400 legionaries and many sailors died.

sides.strength: detachments of the 13th legion and marines

battle.significance: Left Caesar confined until the relief army arrived.

events.title: Mithridates of Pergamon storms Pelusium
events.summary: A relief army raised in Syria and Cilicia by Mithridates of Pergamon, reinforced by 3,000 Jewish troops under Antipater and Arabs and Nabataeans, stormed Pelusium in a single day and marched up the Delta, defeating an Egyptian force near the 'Camp of the Jews' and joining Caesar for the Battle of the Nile.

sides.strength: Syrian, Cilician, Jewish and Arab troops

events.title: Caesar and Cleopatra on the Nile
events.summary: After the Battle of the Nile, Caesar made Cleopatra co-ruler with her younger brother Ptolemy XIV, gave Cyprus back to Egypt, and, according to Suetonius and Appian, cruised up the Nile with her in the royal barge with 400 ships nearly to Ethiopia before his soldiers protested. Their son Ptolemy Caesar (Caesarion) was born in June 47.
events.debate: The Nile cruise is doubted by some as romantic embroidery; Caesarion's paternity was contested by Caesar's partisans (Oppius wrote a pamphlet denying it).

events.title: Caesar's settlement of Judaea
events.summary: Caesar confirmed Hyrcanus II as high priest and ethnarch, made Antipater a Roman citizen exempt from taxes and procurator of Judaea, permitted the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls, restored Joppa, and granted the Jews exemption from military service and other privileges that Josephus records from a series of decrees.
events.detail: These privileges became the charter of Jewish communities across the empire, cited for centuries. Antipater appointed his sons Phasael and Herod governors of Jerusalem and Galilee; Herod's summary execution of the bandit chief Hezekiah got him summoned before the Sanhedrin.

events.title: Dolabella's debt agitation
events.summary: The tribune Publius Cornelius Dolabella, Cicero's son-in-law, proposed cancellation of debts and rents in Caesar's absence; his rival Trebellius opposed him, and their gangs fought in the Forum. Antony, as Master of Horse, sent in troops, killing 800 people. Caesar's return settled the matter with limited rent relief.

events.title: Varro's Antiquities
events.summary: Marcus Terentius Varro dedicated the forty-one books of his Antiquitates rerum humanarum et divinarum, the last sixteen on Roman religion, to Caesar as pontifex maximus. Lost except for fragments, mainly through Augustine's City of God, it was the foundation of all later knowledge of Roman religious institutions.
events.detail: Varro arranged Roman religion under the headings of men, places, times and rites, and distinguished the theology of the poets, of the philosophers and of the state. He is credited with fixing the 'Varronian' foundation date of Rome at 753, which this atlas uses. His output, some 74 works in 620 books, was proverbial; his De lingua Latina (c. 43) partly survives.
events.debate: Date of publication (47 or 46) is uncertain.

events.title: Manoeuvres and battle at Uzitta
events.summary: For weeks Caesar and Metellus Scipio, joined by Juba with elephants, faced each other before Uzitta south of Ruspina, building lines of fortifications; a cavalry and infantry clash in which Labienus was nearly trapped was inconclusive. Caesar trained his men to fight elephants with animals imported from Italy.

battle.significance: A war of position before Thapsus.

events.title: Sittius takes Cirta; Numidia becomes Africa Nova
events.summary: While Caesar fought Scipio, the Campanian adventurer Publius Sittius and King Bocchus II of Mauretania invaded Juba's kingdom and took Cirta, forcing Juba to divide his forces. After Thapsus Caesar annexed most of Numidia as the province of Africa Nova under Sallust as governor and gave Sittius' men the territory of Cirta.
events.detail: Sallust's governorship ended in charges of extortion from which Caesar shielded him; he retired to write history in the famous gardens on the Quirinal paid for, his enemies said, by Africa. Sittius' colonists at Cirta formed the nucleus of the later Cirtan confederation of four colonies.

events.title: Sittius destroys Metellus Scipio's flight at Hippo Regius
events.summary: After Thapsus, Metellus Scipio fled by sea for Spain; storms drove his ships into Hippo Regius, where Sittius' fleet overwhelmed them. Scipio stabbed himself and threw himself overboard, telling those who asked for the general: 'The general is well.'

battle.significance: Ended the career of the Pompeian commander-in-chief.

events.title: Suicide pact of Juba and Petreius at Zama
events.summary: Refused entry by his own city of Zama, where he had built a pyre to burn his family and treasure, King Juba I and the Pompeian legate Marcus Petreius fought a duel so as to die honourably; Petreius was killed, and Juba had a slave kill him.

events.title: Caesar cuts the grain dole
events.summary: Caesar ordered a street-by-street census of grain recipients through the landlords of tenement blocks, reducing the number from 320,000 to 150,000 and filling vacancies by lot from those not registered. He also sent 80,000 poor citizens to overseas colonies.
events.debate: Some scholars think the 320,000 figure counted all male citizens in Rome and the cut was smaller; the closed list of 150,000 remained a model for Augustus' 200,000.

events.title: Caesar's laws of 46: provinces, juries and luxury
events.summary: Caesar limited praetorian governorships to one year and consular to two, removed the tribuni aerarii from juries, dissolved most collegia except ancient ones and Jewish synagogues, raised penalties for violence and treason, and passed a sumptuary law policed by inspectors in the markets.

events.title: Pro Marcello: Cicero breaks his silence
events.summary: When Caesar, at the Senate's plea, pardoned his bitter enemy Marcus Claudius Marcellus, consul of 51, Cicero broke a long silence with a speech of thanks that urged Caesar to heal the state's wounds. Marcellus was murdered at Piraeus on his way home in 45. Pro Ligario followed in the same autumn.

events.title: Cleopatra in Rome
events.summary: Cleopatra, with Ptolemy XIV and probably Caesarion, came to Rome in 46 and lived in Caesar's gardens across the Tiber, where she was formally recognised as a friend and ally. Cicero, who met her about books she had promised him, wrote 'I hate the queen'. She left soon after the Ides of March.
events.debate: Whether she stayed continuously from 46 to 44 or made two visits is disputed.

events.title: Laberius and Publilius Syrus: the mime contest
events.summary: At Caesar's games the elderly equestrian mime-writer Decimus Laberius was induced to act in his own mime, losing caste, and lamented in a prologue that he left home a knight and would return an actor; Caesar then gave the prize to the Syrian freedman Publilius, whose collection of moral one-line maxims (sententiae) became a school text.

events.title: Revolt of Caecilius Bassus in Syria
events.summary: Quintus Caecilius Bassus, a Pompeian survivor of Pharsalus, engineered the murder of Caesar's governor of Syria, Sextus Julius Caesar, at Tyre, won over his legion, and held out at Apamea for three years with Arab and Parthian help against Antistius Vetus and Statius Murcus. His troops joined Cassius in 43.

events.title: Caesar's gold: the aurei of Hirtius
events.summary: In 46 Caesar's praetor Aulus Hirtius struck large issues of aurei (C CAESAR COS TER / A HIRTIVS PR) at 40 to the Roman pound, from the gold of Gaul and the civil war, to pay the triumphal donatives of 5,000 denarii a soldier. It made the aureus, worth 25 denarii, a regular denomination for the first time.

events.title: Cicero's Brutus: a history of Roman oratory
events.summary: In early 46 Cicero wrote the Brutus, a dialogue with Brutus and Atticus surveying some two hundred Roman orators from the earliest times to Hortensius, who had just died, and himself. It is the first history of Latin literature and contains Cicero's account of his own training. The Orator followed later that year.

events.title: Dedication of the Forum Iulium and Temple of Venus Genetrix
events.summary: On 26 September 46, the last day of his triumphal games, Caesar dedicated his new forum, unfinished, with the temple of Venus Genetrix that he had vowed at Pharsalus. The temple contained a statue of Venus by Arcesilaus, paintings of Ajax and Medea by Timomachus, cabinets of engraved gems, a British pearl corselet, and a gilded statue of Cleopatra beside the goddess.
events.detail: The Forum Iulium was a colonnaded rectangle about 160 by 75 metres with the temple at its north-west end, the template for the imperial fora of Augustus, Vespasian, Nerva and Trajan. Its message was dynastic: Venus Genetrix was the mother of Aeneas and so of the Julii. An equestrian statue of Caesar stood in front of the temple, on a horse said to have had human forefeet. Caesar's plan to receive the Senate seated before the temple, without rising, was remembered as one of the gestures that turned opinion against him. The complex was completed by Augustus and rebuilt after the fire of AD 80 by Domitian and Trajan, whose rebuild of the temple and Basilica Argentaria survives in part today.
scholarship: Ulrich, 'Julius Caesar and the creation of the Forum Iulium', AJA 97 (1993)
Westall, 'The Forum Iulium as representation of imperator Caesar', MDAI(R) 103 (1996)
events.debate: Date of the temple's design (begun 54 as a forum, temple added after the Pharsalus vow) and the meaning of Cleopatra's statue are debated.

events.title: Siege of Ategua
events.summary: Caesar opened his Spanish campaign by besieging Ategua, a Pompeian depot east of Corduba, in midwinter. Gnaeus Pompeius failed to relieve it; the garrison commander massacred pro-Caesarian citizens before the town surrendered on 19 February. The anonymous Bellum Hispaniense gives vivid details of sling bullets and burning fascines.

events.title: Caesar storms Corduba and Munda
events.summary: After Munda, Caesar's legate Fabius Maximus besieged Munda town, walled, the Bellum Hispaniense says, with enemy corpses and shields, while Caesar stormed Corduba, where factions fought inside; 22,000 were killed. Hispalis and Urso were taken soon after.

events.title: Cicero's philosophical burst
events.summary: After the death of his daughter Tullia in February 45, Cicero retreated to his villas and in about eighteen months wrote a Consolatio, the Hortensius, Academica, De finibus, Tusculan Disputations, De natura deorum, De divinatione, De fato, Cato Maior de senectute, Laelius de amicitia, Topica and De officiis: a Latin encyclopaedia of Hellenistic philosophy.
events.detail: Cicero presented the programme as a service to the state when politics was closed to him; he coined much of the Latin philosophical vocabulary (qualitas, essentia, moralis). The lost Hortensius later converted the young Augustine to philosophy. He told Atticus they were 'copies: they cost little effort, I supply only the words, of which I have plenty'.

events.title: The pamphlet war over Cato
events.summary: After Cato's suicide, Cicero wrote a eulogy, Cato, and Brutus another; Hirtius replied with a critique, and Caesar, during the Munda campaign, wrote two books of Anticato attacking Cato's character, alleging he had sifted his brother's ashes for gold. The exchange made Cato a martyr of the Republic.

events.title: The Tabula Heracleensis: Caesarian municipal regulations
events.summary: A bronze tablet found at Heraclea in Lucania in 1732 preserves regulations, probably from a lex Iulia of about 45, on road maintenance and wheeled traffic in Rome (banned by day except for building and religious purposes), the grain dole register, and the qualifications for municipal councillors in Italy.
events.debate: Whether the text is a single lex Iulia municipalis or a compilation of several measures is disputed.

events.title: Death of Gnaeus Pompeius the Younger
events.summary: Wounded at Munda, Gnaeus Pompeius fled to Carteia, was abandoned when his fleet was destroyed by Caesar's admiral Didius, and was hunted down near Lauro, where he was killed hiding in a cave. His head was exhibited at Hispalis on 12 April.

events.title: Caesar's Spanish triumph
events.summary: In October 45 Caesar triumphed over Spain, a triumph over fellow citizens that offended many; when the tribune Pontius Aquila remained seated as the chariot passed, Caesar mocked him for days. Caesar's legates Fabius Maximus and Pedius were also given triumphs, and Fabius died in office on 31 December, his consular place filled for a few hours by Caninius Rebilus.
events.detail: Cicero joked that in Caninius' consulship nobody had lunch and nothing bad happened, because the consul was so vigilant he never slept.

events.title: Pro rege Deiotaro
events.summary: In November 45 Cicero defended the Galatian king Deiotarus, accused by his grandson of having plotted to murder Caesar when Caesar was his guest in 47, before Caesar in his own house; it was the first Roman trial held in a private house. No verdict is recorded.

events.title: Caesar dines with Cicero at Puteoli
events.summary: On 19 December 45 Caesar, with 2,000 soldiers, visited Cicero's villa near Puteoli, took a bath and an emetic, dined well and talked of literature, not politics. Cicero wrote to Atticus that it was not the sort of guest to whom one says 'come again when you are passing'.

events.title: Charter of the Colonia Genetiva Iulia at Urso
events.summary: Bronze tablets found at Osuna in Andalusia in 1870-71 preserve much of the charter given to Caesar's colony of Urso, drafted on Caesar's instructions and passed under Antony after his death: rules for magistrates, priesthoods, games, militia, and the admission of freedmen to the council.
events.debate: The surviving copy was engraved in the Flavian period and may include later updates.

events.title: Caesar's portrait on the coinage
events.summary: Early in 44 the moneyers of the year, among them Marcus Mettius and Publius Sepullius Macer, struck denarii with Caesar's laureate (later veiled) head and the legend CAESAR DICT QVART, then CAESAR DICT PERPETVO, the first portrait of a living Roman on the city coinage. The change of title on the dies lets numismatists date issues within weeks of the Ides.
events.detail: The Senate's decree authorising the portrait was among the extravagant honours of early 44 that Dio lists. Hellenistic kings had put their heads on coins for centuries; for Romans it was a royal gesture. The series also shows Venus with Victory, the clasped hands of concord, and the wreath Caesar wore. After the Ides, coin portraits of the triumvirs, the Liberators and Sextus Pompey became normal, and the imperial coinage followed directly.
scholarship: Alföldi, Caesar in 44 v. Chr. II (1974)

events.title: Caesar's planned Getic and Parthian war
events.summary: Caesar planned to leave Rome on 18 March 44 for a three-year war, first against Burebista's Dacians and then against Parthia to avenge Crassus, with sixteen legions and 10,000 cavalry; Octavius and Agrippa were sent ahead to Apollonia to join the army. A Sibylline oracle that only a king could conquer Parthia fed rumours that Caesar would be named king outside Italy.

events.title: Antony takes the treasure in the temple of Ops
events.summary: Antony took possession of Caesar's papers and of 700 million sesterces Caesar had deposited in the temple of Ops for his campaigns, using both to buy support; Cicero accused him of forging decrees in Caesar's name and selling privileges, such as citizenship for all Sicilians and the restoration of Deiotarus.
events.locName: Temple of Ops, Capitol or Forum

events.title: Lex Antonia abolishes the dictatorship
events.summary: Early in the period after the Ides, Antony carried a law abolishing the dictatorship forever, a popular gesture of reconciliation. The office was never revived; Augustus refused it in 22 BC when the people tried to force it on him.

events.title: Cicero's De officiis
events.summary: In autumn 44, between the Second and later Philippics, Cicero wrote De officiis for his son, then studying in Athens: three books on duties, adapting the Stoic Panaetius, arguing that the honourable and the useful never conflict and that Caesar's tyranny was the supreme example of crime passing for utility.
events.detail: It became the most widely read work of moral philosophy in Latin for 1,500 years: the second book printed after the Gutenberg Bible, and a manual for Renaissance and Enlightenment gentlemen. Its denunciation of Caesar shows how the treatise was also a political pamphlet.

events.title: The lynching of the poet Helvius Cinna
events.summary: At Caesar's funeral the crowd, inflamed by Antony's speech, took the tribune and poet Gaius Helvius Cinna, a friend of Caesar, for the praetor Lucius Cornelius Cinna, who had praised the assassins, and tore him to pieces, carrying his head on a spear.
events.detail: Cinna's short epic Zmyrna, nine years in the making, was praised by Catullus (poem 95) as a masterpiece that would outlast the bulky annals of his rivals; only a few lines survive. Shakespeare's 'I am Cinna the poet' scene comes straight from Plutarch.

events.title: The Ludi Apollinares of Brutus
events.summary: Brutus, as urban praetor, paid for lavish Games of Apollo in July 44 but dared not attend; he had hoped that a performance of Accius' Tereus would win applause for the Liberators. Octavian then staged Games for Caesar's Victory, during which the comet appeared.

events.title: The Martia and Fourth legions defect to Octavian
events.summary: Antony brought four Macedonian legions to Brundisium, where he executed centurions of the Martia for insubordination; Octavian, who had raised 3,000 veterans in Campania on his own authority, outbid him with 500 denarii a man. The Legio Martia and Legio IV went over to Octavian at Alba Fucens, and Cicero hailed the boy in the Senate.
events.detail: This was the moment Octavian became a military power. Raising a private army was illegal, and Cicero's Third Philippic of 20 December retrospectively praised it as saving the state, a precedent the Res Gestae opens with: 'At the age of nineteen, on my own initiative and at my own expense, I raised an army.'

events.title: Dolabella murders Trebonius at Smyrna
events.summary: Publius Cornelius Dolabella, on his way to Syria, entered Smyrna by night, seized Gaius Trebonius, proconsul of Asia and one of the conspirators, tortured him for two days and beheaded him, the first of the assassins to die. The Senate declared Dolabella a public enemy.

events.title: Cassius besieges Dolabella at Laodicea
events.summary: Cassius, who had taken over all eight legions in Syria, besieged Dolabella in Laodicea-on-Sea; the city was betrayed and Dolabella had a soldier kill him. Cassius then fined Laodicea and Tarsus heavily.

battle.significance: Made Cassius master of the East.

events.title: Death of Decimus Brutus
events.summary: Deserted by his legions after Plancus joined Antony, Decimus Brutus tried to reach Macedonia through the Alps and Illyricum disguised as a Gaul, but was captured by a Gallic chieftain, Camilus, and killed on Antony's orders. He had been the first conspirator to be honoured and the first to fall in the field.

events.title: Lepidus joins Antony at Forum Iulii
events.summary: Antony, retreating from Mutina, crossed the Alps to Narbonensis. On 29 May 43, after the soldiers of Lepidus, governor of Narbonensis and Nearer Spain, fraternised with Antony's at the Pons Argenteus, Lepidus joined him, writing to the Senate that his troops had compelled him. The Senate declared him a public enemy.
events.detail: Cicero's correspondence with Plancus, Pollio and Lepidus in May and June 43 lets us watch the Senate's position dissolve as the western governors, with seventeen legions between them, joined Antony one after another. Plancus' letters are a masterpiece of hedging. Decimus Brutus, abandoned, fled and was killed.

events.title: Lex Pedia: the assassins condemned
events.summary: Octavian's colleague and cousin Quintus Pedius carried a law setting up a court to try Caesar's murderers in absence; all were condemned and outlawed, including Sextus Pompey, who had not been involved. The same month a lex curiata confirmed Octavian's adoption as Caesar's son.

events.title: Plancus founds Lugdunum
events.summary: Lucius Munatius Plancus, governor of Gallia Comata, founded the colony of Lugdunum (Lyon) on the hill of Fourvière above the confluence of Rhône and Saône, on Senate's orders, for Roman refugees expelled from Vienna by the Allobroges. It became the capital of the Three Gauls and seat of the imperial mint.
events.detail: Plancus' tomb at Gaeta records the foundation of Lugdunum and of Raurica (Augst). The site, a Celtic oppidum named after the god Lugus, had a natural strategic position for routes to the Rhine, the Atlantic and the Mediterranean. Augustus made it the hub of Agrippa's Gallic road network and in 12 BC the altar of Rome and Augustus was dedicated there.

events.title: The EID MAR denarius of Brutus
events.summary: Brutus' moneyer Lucius Plaetorius Cestianus struck a denarius showing Brutus' head and, on the reverse, a cap of liberty between two daggers with the legend EID MAR. Dio describes it, and it is the most famous coin of antiquity; fewer than a hundred silver examples and three gold aurei are known.
events.detail: The coin is a paradox: a self-proclaimed defender of liberty putting his own portrait on coinage, exactly as Caesar had. The pileus was the cap given to freed slaves, so the message is that Rome had been freed by the daggers. It was struck in 43-42 to pay the Liberators' army before Philippi. Many examples on the market are forgeries; an aureus sold in 2020 for over 3 million pounds.
events.locName: travelling mint of Brutus, Macedonia or Asia

events.title: Cassius takes Rhodes
events.summary: Rhodes refused to join the Liberators; Cassius defeated its fleet twice off Myndus and Cnidus, blockaded the city and took it without a fight, executing fifty leaders, stripping the temples and confiscating 8,500 talents. Brutus meanwhile sacked Xanthus in Lycia.

sides.strength: fleet of c. 80 ships and army

events.title: Plancus rebuilds the Temple of Saturn
events.summary: Lucius Munatius Plancus rebuilt the Temple of Saturn in the Forum, seat of the state treasury, from spoils of an Alpine campaign, as recorded on an inscription. The eight Ionic columns standing today belong to a fourth-century restoration on Plancus' podium.

sources.r: Plancus at the Temple of Saturn

events.title: Murcus and Ahenobarbus destroy the triumviral convoy
events.summary: On the day of the first battle of Philippi the Liberators' admirals Statius Murcus and Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus intercepted Domitius Calvinus' convoy bringing two legions, including the Martia, across the Adriatic, and destroyed it; many soldiers burned with their ships. News arrived too late to stop Brutus giving battle again.

battle.significance: A victory that could have starved the triumvirs had Brutus waited.

events.title: Antony in Ephesus: the levy on Asia
events.summary: Entering Ephesus as the new Dionysus, Antony demanded that the cities of Asia pay in one year the tribute of nine (then reduced to two years' worth payable in two), to pay the 170,000 men of the triumviral armies. He rewarded cities that had resisted the Liberators, such as Laodicea and Tarsus, and summoned Cleopatra to Tarsus.
